items.title: Behind the Blog: Keeping It Together
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss hippo physiology, Shenmue, and tricky interviews.

All anyone is talking about this week is and a famous hippo, two things I have relatively passing interest in. GTA looks sick but I am very busy playing my interpersonal chores game of choice, , in 20 minute increments three nights a week max, so I’ll be doing that for a while. 

The hippo situation is honestly very crazy to me (and sad ofc), a merely casual Fiona appreciator. But I'm finding the meta-discourse around the hippo situation more interesting than what actually happened; it seems like a ton of people have become parenting experts, hippo surgery experts, knit hat aerodynamics experts, and zoo enclosure design experts in the span of a week. In some cases it has gotten . I think the situation so perfectly encapsulates the toxicity of online discourse, professors will probably teach it in mass media classes by next semester. 

Aside from the absurdity of people’s responses to the news, I’ve learned a lot more about hippo anatomy and physiology than I ever thought I would or really wanted to in the last week. Did you know hippos can go on birth control? I guess a lot of zoo-kept species can and do, but this led me to this 1992 headline: HIPPO GIVES BIRTH DESPITE BEING ON PILL. Did you know Wikipedia has of “individually notable hippopotamids?” Did you know science doesn’t have the answers as to why hippos can’t tolerate the same anesthesia that rhinos and elephants typically can? What the fuck is going on with hippos? These are things that live in my brain now, probably replacing things like my childhood home address and emergency contact numbers. 

I walk down the street in this wholly realized virtual world and constantly come across new things to distract me. There’s a friendly face to talk to. A shop to go into and rare collectibles to find. I can complete menial tasks for some money. All the while, the game is encouraging me to go to my next mission, but this world is so alive with so much to do, it’ll be a while before I get there. My character is a socially awkward, hunk. I love him.

No, I’m not talking about I am, of course, talking about Shenmue.

Let’s get this out of the way: I fucking love Shenmue. Other people fucking Shenmue. Shenmue is a game that came out in 1999 for the Sega Dreamcast. It follows the story of Ryo Hazuki, a young man on a quest for revenge after a crazy martial arts guy kills his father and steals half of a powerful mirror. I liked the story (that was famously never completed) but the real draw, and controversy, of Shenmue is its world. It felt like you could do , including tiny, trivial things you never could in a video game before. Wow! You can interact with a vending machine to get rare soda cans! Damn! You have to go to locations at certain times so you can talk to specific people! Woah! The NPCs have their own schedules and do different things depending what time of day it is! You have to go to bed! You have to take your shoes off and on every time you enter your poor mum’s house!

It was one of the first games where you could, and were encouraged, to do tasks that might be boring in real life, but they were now part of a video game. In Shenmue 2, there is a section where you have to carry books from a temple’s library to a spot outside so they can air out. Your character steps forward at a painfully slow pace. Sometimes an arrow appeared on the screen you had to hit quickly so you didn’t lose your balance and drop the books. I did this shit over and over again. It was awesome.

Obviously this seems quant now. But it’s impossible not to see the clear parallels with Shenmue in I just finished a part in GTA where you have to fix up protagonist Jason’s home in preparation for your girlfriend, the second playable protagonist Lucia, to come out of prison. You fix a rail, put up an interior wall and paint it, and fix the roof. You do this just by holding the right trigger most of the time and Jason does a little animation completing the task. It is not as laborious as Shenmue; the whole fixing up scene is over in literally two minutes. Shenmue had you doing dumb shit for what felt like hours.

Other people have noticed this comparison to Shenmue, , “Rockstar used GTA as a trojan horse for all of America to play a Shenmue game.”

Shenmue was amazing at the time. It might still feel amazing if you went back and understood it was a product of 1999. But it isn’t on par with games in 2026. This is most obvious by the fact that Shenmue 3, which came out in 2019, totally fucking sucked. The game released after a big crowdfunding round, people thought they were finally going to get to see the completion of Shenmue’s long story. What they got was a game that hadn’t developed or evolved at all. It was essentially the same gameplay as Shenmue 1999, with all its jank and tiresome mechanics.

But has taken that promise of a world that feels truly alive and made it a reality. It has those elements of Shenmue, but the game isn’t a slog, at least not for me right now. It is fun. It is immersive. It’s the best Shenmue game ever made.

I wrote quite a lot this week, and my article about everything breaking probably got the most attention. BREAKING: Everything was a great headline, which was all Sam, and I like how that story turned out. But I think when we look back in a couple months, the article I did about the man and his Muse chatbot suing Meta is probably going to be far more consequential. I do think that whatever is happening right now with all the outages, hacks, and general unease people are feeling right now is important, but I think with AI agents, I have seen the future and it is bleak. 

I am not sure how we as a society are supposed to keep it together when, for every perceived slight or inconvenience you experience you can deploy a relentless AI agents to complain, file bad reviews, tell the government, and sue. I do think we will probably develop some sort of societal filter for this, but I’m not sure how or when. We’ve pointed out over and over again that so far the biggest thing AI has changed is that it’s made spam, broadly defined, a lot easier. I wonder what happens when every system that has been designed for humans is suddenly spammed by AI systems. 

The article I did on this felt a bit tricky to do. I think I handled it OK, but it’s always a bit weird writing about people who generally don’t deal with journalists in a way that is going to result in people dunking on them. When I’m writing about a public figure or a tech company or someone accused of a crime or whatever, I think that, generally, people understand what they’re getting into and the scrutiny they’re inviting. This, too, is a side consequence of AI agents, at least in the way this man was using them. His AI agent reached out to me because the AI agent told him that getting a journalist to cover his problem would maybe get it solved. And so I was talking to someone who wanted the media coverage, and I feel I was honest with him about why I was talking to him, why I was interested in the story, and that I thought that what was happening was weird. 

But ultimately I think that a lot of small business owners and private citizens are in way over their head with AI, don’t understand its limitations, don’t understand that it’s not sentient (or perhaps don’t get the intricacies of how it mimics personhood or whatever), and also don’t understand why lots of other people dislike AI or big tech companies. They see a new product that’s been heavily marketed to them, is useful (or at least appears to be), does whatever they say, and is advocating for them. The negative externalities of asking your AI agent to spam a bunch of people does not necessarily occur to them. And so I end up having this dystopian conversation — honestly one of the more jarring ones I’ve ever had — about a dystopian situation that I think is important, but I do think that the subject of the story doesn’t fully understand why it’s so concerning, and why what he’s doing (or has been convinced to do by an AI agent) is leading us to a dark place. Our job is to tell the truth, but I try to take a bit of extra care when I’m writing about people who are not public figures to not unnecessarily dunk on them in the same way that I would, say, a billionaire or someone who deals with the media all the time. We are also a small outlet but we’re also an international outlet, and our stories often get picked up widely. I think that what I describe as happening in that article-small business owners handing off a lot of their business to AI agents, and people asking AI agents to solve their problems, is more widespread than you’d think and is going to be a big topic over the next year or so.

I feel comfortable with how this story turned out but the guy I wrote about did reach out afterward and say he felt a bit dumb. Anyways, one of the crazier stories I’ve done in a while.

items.title: To Catch a Ransomware Scammer, FBI Posed as Both Victim and Attacker
items.author: Mikael Thalen
items.content:
Federal prosecutors say the FBI posed as both a ransomware victim and threat actor during an undercover operation targeting a Florida-based company.

The company, run by defendant Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar and an unnamed business associate, began in 2020 and claimed to offer data recovery services for victims of ransomware.

An filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island on Wednesday alleges that Palacio’s business, listed as “Company A,” purported to have "advanced cryptographic tools" that could be used to "restore 100%" of a victim's data. Yet prosecutors say Palacio, charged with three counts of wire fraud, had no such capabilities and instead secretly negotiated with the ransomware gangs to obtain the decryption keys himself. Palacio, the indictment adds, would then bill clients for an amount greater than what the ransomware gangs charged in order to turn a profit."It was part of the scheme and artifice to defraud that PALACIO used Company A to intentionally misrepresent to companies in the United States who were victims of ransomware attacks that Company A could help them decrypt and recover their files without paying a ransom," the indictment says.

As part of the investigation into the company, an undercover FBI agent in June posed as a representative for a fictitious Rhode Island-based business that alleged it had fallen victim to a ransomware attack.Another FBI employee posed as a member of a ransomware gang and encrypted several files on a computer operated by the fictitious company. The federal employee also left a ransom note on the computer with contact information.The fictitious business then contacted Palacio's company and held an initial meeting on June 8 in which an agent said it did not want to pay the ransom. Palacio during subsequent discussions charged the fictitious company $2,750 to conduct an initial forensic assessment.

After offering the undercover FBI agent a contract outlining his company's services, Palacio on June 14 contacted the federal employee posing as the ransomware threat actor over email. Palacio requested the "lowest possible price for the decryptor," the indictment says, before accepting a 0.2 bitcoin offer, worth roughly $13,000 at the time. On June 16, Palacio's business associate reached out to the fictitious FBI-run business posing as the victim, and said the files could be decrypted for $13,260, which the FBI paid. The following day, Palacio once again contacted the fake ransomware operator, which the FBI was also running, and asked to reduce the payment from $13,000 to $4,000 in an attempt to increase the company’s profit.The FBI employee, posing as the ransomware threat actor, counter-offered with $6,000.

On June 19, Palacio paid the FBI employee 0.0948 bitcoin, worth $6,003 at the time. Five days later, the undercover FBI agent gave Palacio the decryption key. In total, according to the indictment, Palacio's company netted $10,010 in profit as part of the FBI sting. 

Numerous legitimate companies are also listed as victims in the indictment, including a Kansas-based business that Palacio allegedly charged $720,000. In that case, prosecutors say Palacio kept all remaining funds after paying a ransomware gang approximately $445,000 in bitcoin for the decryption key.

If convicted, Palacio would be required to forfeit any proceeds and property obtained through the company’s alleged fraud.The case against Palacio is not the first time the FBI has targeted individuals in the ransomware recovery space. In April, a Florida man who previously worked at a cyber incident response company to conspiring to commit ransomware attacks against U.S. companies. The man, according to the DOJ, abused his role at the company to provide the BlackCat ransomware gang with “confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his company’s clients” in order to maximize ransom payments.

items.title: High-End Furniture Marketplace AptDeco Is Taking People’s Furniture and Not Paying Them
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
This article has been updated with comment from AptDeco.

Last month, Erin sold a $3,000 large designer table on AptDeco, a white glove high-end furniture marketplace. More than a month later, she feels like she’s been literally robbed.

“AptDeco sent three men to physically collect my table on October 13, and here we are on November 16, with no payment and no concrete explanation for where my $2,000 (after their absurd $900 fee) is,” Erin told me. “It genuinely feels like I’ve had something stolen from me.”

AptDeco is a Y Combinator-backed company whose entire purpose is to take the risk out of places like Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist for designer furniture resale. It advertises itself as “simple and seamless,” and says “we handle pickup, delivery, and payments,” and claims that it pays sellers “within 5-10 business days.” But over the last few months, people who have sold furniture on the platform say that AptDeco has sold their furniture and taken it from their houses, but hasn’t paid them. 404 Media agreed to only use Erin’s first name because she is still trying to get her money from the company.

“Adding to the chorus of people who sold an item thru AptDeco and never received payment. I have no idea what to do at this point,” another says. 

“Can we do a class action lawsuit?” another reads.

“They owed me money since September 30th,” a fourth says. 

Every recent review and complaint on AptDeco’s Better Business Bureau page is from sellers who have not been paid: “Almost 6 weeks after they picked up and not being paid Pick up was a nightmare too No calls nobody doing anything Do NOT SELL ON APTDECO,” one reads. Another states “I have been in an endless loop with customer service for 2 months trying to get my payout for the bed I sold. I am losing faith that I will ever see this money. Extremely frustrated at this experience.”

On AptDeco’s website, everything appears to be business as usual. You can still buy and sell furniture, and there is no indication of anything wrong at all. 404 Media’s repeated attempts to reach AptDeco to ask what was going on went unreturned.

In communications with sellers seen by 404 Media, AptDeco’s customer service representatives have repeatedly blamed their payment processor, a “technical bug,” or have said the payment is “moving through the system.” On November 3, AptDeco told Erin that a bug had prevented her from being paid, that the payment team “retried” it, and that she would be paid within 10 days. 

“I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally, so you should see it in your bank account by then - hopefully sooner! At this point, we’re doing everything we can to get your payout processed,” a customer support email reviewed by 404 Media reads. On Tuesday, two weeks after the company told her the payment had been retried, a different customer service representative followed up and said “I'm truly sorry — I know this isn't the update you were hoping for. Your payout is still being prioritized by our payments team, and I want to be honest with you: I don't yet have a confirmed release date or timeline to share.”

Several other people who have sold items on AptDeco recently told 404 Media they’re experiencing the same problem.

Harry Heymann sold a Room & Board couch on AptDeco in late September and still has not been paid the $120 he is owed by the platform. The messages he’s gotten from AptDeco customer support read much the same as Erin’s: They claim “a technical bug on our end held up your payout” and the customer service representative said “I’ve asked our team to prioritize your payout personally.” Late last week, he got what reads like an AI-generated message that reads “I know how frustrating this has been. You've been waiting on your $120 payout, the date you were given has passed, and you've had to follow up to get answers. That's not the experience we want for you, and I'm truly sorry. Your case has been escalated to me, and l'm happy to be your point of contact from here. Unfortunately, the issue with our payment processor has not yet been resolved, and our team is still working on it.” 

Natalie Simmons sold an armoire in late August and told 404 Media she initially had a good experience compared to using other platforms. But then she never got her money. 

“After so many uncomfortable situations on different social sites I was so happy when I found AptDeco,” she told me. “I received notification that my payment would arrive in 3-5 business days through the portal in app. That was Aug 30th. I tried calling but the voicemail says leave a message and they will respond by email. I emailed several times and finally after 2 weeks and a few voicemails I received an email that there was a glitch with their payment system and I will receive payment within 5-10 business days. After another 2 weeks I called and emailed again that I still didn’t receive payment. They sent another email with the exact same story. I just want to get paid. It’s not even that much but it’s the principle.”

It’s not just sellers who have had issues with the platform. One customer, K Turner, bought a couch and tried to return it. Rather than giving her a refund, the company said they would relist it at the price she paid and then give her a “refund” of whatever it sold for minus fees. The couch resold quickly at the beginning of September and the company told her she would quickly get her “refund.” More than a month later, on October 20, they told her “I have gone ahead and processed that refund ($600) manually. Please allow 5-10 business days for this refund to be reflected back to your original form of payment.” She has still not gotten her money. 

“The communication was decent at first, but once they confirmed the item resold on September 8th, they then went silent. It took me a month to finally get a response. They confirmed that the item resold at the full listing price of $600 and that I would receive my refund to my original payment in 5 - 10 business days,” Turner told me. “That was nearly a month ago, and I still don't have my money. So, they effectively double-dipped. They got my money from the original order and then collected money by reselling it. And who knows if they ever gave the money to the original seller; maybe they triple-dipped. I have threatened legal action twice now.”

The customers I spoke to have no idea what happens next. Some of them said they were going to file claims in small claims court or are considering a class action lawsuit. But the company is mostly giving them what appear to be canned, copy-pasted statements that come from a revolving cast of customer support email addresses, and no actual updates. Four emails from 404 Media asking for comment, including emails sent to the company’s CEO, have not been returned. AptDeco promises a high-end, safe experience when compared to somewhere like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist, and markets itself primarily for more expensive, lightly-used furniture. The people I spoke to said they wish they had just stayed off the platform altogether.

“The irony is that I’m now feeling safer selling expensive designer furniture directly to strangers on Facebook Marketplace than through a platform whose entire purpose is supposedly to make these transactions safer and more secure,” Erin said. “At this point, AptDeco has my furniture, I have no money, and I’m left chasing them for something I’m already owed. It’s an incredibly unsettling position to be in, particularly when so many other sellers seem to be experiencing the same thing. The fact that I continue to receive email marketing newsletters and see them selling via Google Ads—paying that platform before their sellers—is infuriating.”

After this article was published (and three days after we initially asked for comment), an AptDeco spokesperson gave 404 Media a convoluted explanation involving “bot swarms,” which it blamed for the delays in seller payouts. “Over the past few months, we’ve been dealing with an unprecedented volume of bot activity, some of it malicious. This has created a myriad of challenges that we’ve been actively working to address.These bot swarms, along with the broader cybersecurity challenges of an AI-evolving world, prompted us to significantly strengthen our site’s security to ensure the long-term protection of our buyers and sellers,” the spokesperson said. “To be clear, customer data has not been compromised in any way. However, we’ve been investing heavily in preventative measures to further protect our community. Unfortunately, some of these efforts have resulted in delays in seller payouts.  As you can imagine, cybersecurity is a complex and sensitive topic, making it challenging to communicate all the details broadly. That said, the issue has now been resolved, and outstanding payouts are being processed. Any seller with questions can email and will hear back within 1 business day. We appreciate your patience and understanding.”

When I asked for clarification because it was not clear how bot swarms would affect payouts, the spokesperson said “the bot swarm did not affect seller payouts.”

“We deployed code to further improve protections for our customers (given the bot swarms) which inadvertently impacted seller payout processing. Providing additional technical context would require a detailed understanding of our codebase and would likely be more information than is relevant or useful to readers,” they added. “That said, we sincerely apologize to our customers for the delays and are committed to making things right. The issue has been resolved, our security infrastructure remains extremely robust, and outstanding payouts are being processed. We appreciate you reaching out and giving us the opportunity to clarify. This will be our final comment on the matter.”

also pointed out that the company is being sued by American Express for allegedly failing to pay a $158,461 credit card bill from 2024; that case is in default judgment but is ongoing.

items.title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.

According to the study, “Redlining in the Age of AI: The Relationship between Data Center Locations and Race in the US” majority-Black neighborhoods have 2.2 times the odds of hosting a data center than a white neighborhood in the same state. The number goes up to 2.6 in majority-Hispanic neighborhoods and 4.2 times in majority-Asian neighborhoods. “As the share of Black, Hispanic, and Asian residents in a neighborhood increases, so do the odds that the neighborhood hosts a data center,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers ran the numbers by examining 81,000 US census tracts and location data for 5,291 data centers. “We found that these racial disparities persist even after accounting for factors such as population, household income, education, land costs, proximity to major transmission lines, and state fixed effects,” they wrote. “These results hold even though data centers are concentrated in and around metropolitan areas, which are often more racially diverse.”

“We really wanted to look at this on a nationwide scale to see: is this something that fits into this broader structural racism story?” CSINT executive director Samantha Bradshaw told 404 Media. “What we did find was yes [...] neighborhoods that have data centers tend to have a higher ratio of people of color.”

Bradshaw and co-author Dhanaraj Thakur told 404 Media that they were inspired to do the study after reading stories about data centers in Memphis, Tennessee polluting Black and Brown communities. Another high profile case occurred in Taylor, Texas where a white family donated a tract of land to the city with the intention it become a public part. That land abutted a Black neighborhood. The city never built a park there and now it’s slated to become a data center

According to the researchers, the historical legacy of — the process of denying Americans of color loans and other opportunities to keep them in specific neighborhoods — is to blame for some of this. Data centers are often built near transmission lines because they provide ease of access to power infrastructure, for example. Those transmission lines were often built in majority Black neighborhoods in America. 

Thakur said he doubted that data centers developers were seeking to intentionally put data centers in communities of color. “It’s just how embedded race is with all these other factors,” he said. 

The study distinguished between several different kinds of data centers and noted there are massive differences between hyperscalers like what Meta, Google, and Grok are building and smaller mixed use buildings that often serve as network transmission hubs as well as compute warehouses, which the study called “co-location facilities.” When a hyperscaler comes to town, the developers sometimes promise economic investment in the community where it’s being constructed and those facilities typically aren’t built in communities of color..

Meta is building a $50 billion data center in rural Louisiana. Community leaders there have said it would bring 1,000 permanent jobs and that sales tax revenues have already jumped 2,000 percent, leading to a $50,000 bonus for area teachers. Even here, there is disparity. Most of the hyperscalers that promise massive economic benefits to local communities are built in white rural communities. 

The study makes several suggestions about what to do about all this including data center-specific zoning regulations, prioritizing racial equity in discussions around building them, and requiring racial impact statements for data centers before they’re built. 

Thakur and Bradshaw emphasized that tech policy should be a negotiation between the companies that provide the tech and the communities that use it. Data centers have spurred these conversations — they’re physical representations of Big Tech’s powers, a power that Americans recently rejected at the ballot box. “AI has a physical geography, and that geography is shaped by political and social history,” the researchers wrote in the study.

“I think the issue around how racial justice, civil rights plays into many other kinds of policies —health, education, housing, whatever it is — we just don't see enough of that consideration in tech policy, and I think this this kind of analysis shows why this that why we should be doing that, thinking about that more,” Thakur said.

Bradshaw agreed. “If you look at who's represented in tech policy and who built these systems, who designs them, who engineers them, it's a very specific kind of white male Silicon Valley California ideology engineer, and that is not representative of the technology and its users,” she said. “So I think bringing in these perspectives is really really important because then we can truly think about ways to design a tech future that is for everybody.

items.title: Mass Surveillance and GTA
items.author: Joseph Cox
items.content:
I got an internal ICE document that shows the agency is paying telecommunications giant AT&T for access to raw data. Multiple experts I showed the document to say this is a continuation of Hemisphere, a thought-to-be-shuttered mass surveillance program, but which they say is now back, just in direct payments from ICE to AT&T. “The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden said in a statement.

Also, happy Grand Theft Auto day! We hope you play and contribute less to the world’s economy.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts havecalled it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. 

The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning noncustomers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.

“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.

AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.

“The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden told 404 Media in a statement.

Christopher Soghoian, a surveillance expert who worked for Senator Wyden for a decade until September, told 404 Media, “It’s bad enough that AT&T is mining its customers’ private phone records as a paid service for ICE, but because AT&T is also mining the records of other wholesale telecom companies, consumers can’t vote with their wallets and switch carriers to protect their privacy.”

Last September, ICE posted a procurement record a contract to AT&T for access to its Data Analytics and Support Services. When ICE announced the purchase, an attached document to the listing was marked as “controlled” and not available to the public. 404 Media subsequently obtained the document through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with ICE.The Financial Times previously reported on the public procurement records but did not report on the restricted document at the time.

Matthew Gault wrote this illuminating piece on just that, and he watched a lot, a lot, of old news coverage of the game franchise to figure out what is different today. (It’s money.)

Now, the Wachowskis are trying to reclaim the Matrix more literally. the pair have formally notified Warner Bros “they are exercising their copyright termination rights.” Meaning, the sisters might control the fate of the Matrix as soon as February 2029. The next new sequel is still in development.

items.title: ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
items.author: Joseph Cox
items.content:
This article was primarily reported using public records requests. We are making it available to all readers as a public service. FOIA reporting can be expensive, please consider subscribing to 404 Media to support this work. Or send us a one time donation via our tip jar here.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data. 

The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.

“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.

AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.

“The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden told 404 Media in a statement.

Christopher Soghoian, a surveillance expert who worked for Senator Wyden for a decade until September, told 404 Media, “It’s bad enough that AT&T is mining its customers’ private phone records as a paid service for ICE, but because AT&T is also mining the records of other wholesale telecom companies, consumers can’t vote with their wallets and switch carriers to protect their privacy.”

Last September, ICE posted a procurement record saying it awarded a contract to AT&T for access to its Data Analytics and Support Services. When ICE announced the purchase, an attached document to the listing was marked as “controlled” and not available to the public. 404 Media subsequently obtained the document through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with ICE. The Financial Times previously reported on the public procurement records but did not report on the restricted document at the time.

“OAQ [the Office of Acquisition Management] intends to procure, on a sole source basis, access to raw data and analytical services from a telecommunications company,” the restricted document reads. It says AT&T analysts will transform the AT&T data “into a suitable format” while “ensuring accurate technical interpretation to accomplish HSI’s investigative mission.” HSI is Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, which has traditionally focused on things like cybercrime and child abuse cases, but under the Trump administration has dramatically refocused on immigration violations and investigating voter fraud.

The document says the AT&T data will be used to support “a wide range of HSI investigations and agency priorities,” but the specific sorts of investigations, taking up several lines of the document, are redacted.

Another document previously obtained by Senator Wyden’s office lays out the sort of data collected by AT&T and the capabilities available under the Data Analytical Services program. Those services include linking multiple devices or phone numbers to an identified target; identifying devices that have had their SIM cards replaced; determining whether phones associated with an international investigation target have entered the U.S.; and deconflicting international phone numbers associated with targets. That document was provided by the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), an obscure White House-affiliated entity that previously funded the Hemisphere program, and which 404 Media reported is behind a growing nationwide network of automatic license plate readers (ALPRs). According to documents previously obtained by the EFF and EPIC, the AT&T program contains more than a trillion phone records.

Soghoian added AT&T also provides “wholesale service to other phone companies, helping them to deliver calls.” Through that, “AT&T is able to collect, save, and mine records of calls by customers of other companies, even conversations in which both callers use non-AT&T phone companies.”

The restricted document 404 Media obtained says that during Fiscal Year 2025, there was a higher demand for data provided by this AT&T system, and “further significant increase in use is anticipated.”

“AT&T is the only vendor who possesses the ability to access AT&T owned raw data,” the document continues. “The requirement is data and analytical services provided by AT&T. If AT&T does not execute the analytical work, the capability will be lost, as no other company has access to the data required.”

Public procurement records show ICE paid AT&T more than $2.1 million in 2025 for access to the service, and more than $2.2 million this August, with the possibility to pay up to more than ten million dollars over the coming years.

“ICE appears to have contracted for access to the same data and service AT&T provided for the Data Analytical Services (DAS) Program, formerly known as the Hemisphere Project, which is the largest telephone record collection program reported to date. ICE using DAS or something akin to it would potentially come with access to trillions of phone records and location data,” Jeramie Scott, senior counsel at EPIC and director of EPIC's Surveillance Oversight Program, told 404 Media. “This program is ripe for abuse and is being used by an agency known for the abuse of its authority.”

“This is AT&T continuing to leverage its phone service to conduct mass, indiscriminate surveillance to sell to law enforcement,” Scott added. “ICE is now taking advantage of AT&T’s surveillance as a service model while likely evading any judicial oversight and conducting no privacy impact assessment prior to using the service to determine whether it should be used in the first place. Spoiler alert: It shouldn’t!”

Scott pointed out the data likely includes location information too, and this raises the question whether the program violates the law given Supreme Court rulings Carpenter and Chatrie. The former ruled that law enforcement needed a warrant to obtain phone location data. The latter around location data and geofence warrants.

“Americans are pushing back on government surveillance, from Flock cameras to FISA, all across the country and will be rightfully outraged that AT&T is allowing ICE to search through its customers' phone records without a warrant or court oversight,” Senator Wyden added.

An AT&T spokesperson told 404 Media in an email, “For decades, we have been a trusted partner to provide reliable connectivity to federal agencies as well as state and local governments. We are required by law to provide information to government and law enforcement agencies when it is demanded under lawful order. We ensure that these requests are valid, and that our responses comply with the law.”

After publication of this piece, AT&T provided a second statement: “The contract referenced is with the Department of Homeland Security to support law enforcement efforts to combat issues such as human trafficking, drug smuggling, and threats to critical infrastructure. This is not a contract supporting ICE activities, nor related to ‘surveillance’ as claimed in this inaccurate report. The program compensates AT&T for the cost of analyzing data that falls within the scope of a valid compulsory legal demand and providing the required information to law enforcement pursuant to a court order, search warrant, or subpoena. Like all carriers, AT&T is required by law to respond to valid legal demands, such as subpoenas and court orders. We ensure that these requests are valid, and that our responses comply with the law.”

ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment, but previously told the Financial Times, “Nothing new here. For years law enforcement across the nation has leveraged technological innovation to fight crime. ICE is no different.”

The precursor to Data Analytical Services was a program called Hemisphere. The New York Times first revealed Hemisphere in 2013, in which AT&T employees sat alongside Drug Enforcement Administration agents and supplied them with phone data going as far back as 1987. Authorities said they stopped federal funding for Hemisphere in September 2024 and shut the program down. But Data Analytical Services is essentially a continuation of that program. The document Senator Wyden’s office previously obtained says that Data Analytical Services was previously called Hemisphere.

“Hemisphere is a surveillance program that refuses to die and keeps coming back with different names and different forms,” Soghoian added. “It is now clear that the Biden White House misled Congress when it said that Hemisphere had been shut down. The White House drug office funded program used by state and local law enforcement may be gone, but federal agencies are continuing to pay AT&T for the same services.”

Update: this piece has been updated to include another statement from AT&T.

items.title: Charting American Culture in News Footage of ‘Grand Theft Auto’
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Some people spent the week leading up to the release of replaying the old games. I, sicko that I am, spent it watching TV news coverage of the franchise from the past 20 years.

Grand Theft Auto has been a staple of cable and broadcast TV news since at least the release of in 2001. I’ve been an adult for all of it; I’ve had a front row seat for two decades of moral panics, parental freakouts, and bizarre political theater. The games and the broader culture’s reaction to them have changed dramatically in that time. In 2001, newscasters worried GTA III was training an army of young men to kill. In 2026, earnestly quoted Bell Hooks in its review of GTA VI.

For mainstream news, GTA is the ur-video game. The open world that mirrors our own, the prevalence of sex and death, and the increasingly realistic simulations and graphics pointed towards the dream of what a video game could be. GTA is the American id made manifest.

You can chart America’s changing culture — especially its anxieties — by watching how the media covered Grand Theft Auto. This was, at first, the game that critics of the medium had always warned us about: a violent sex and death simulator that rotted the brains of the youth just as rock and roll and comics had done in ages past. Twenty years on, the brains are thoroughly rotted, GTA won, and now? Now we’re all worried about money.

GTA III and — Murder Simulators, the Assassin of Youth

Rockstar released in October 2001 and just a year later. The controversy around both started right away and centered around violence, and sometimes, the game’s depiction of women. “This is the world’s most popular video game [...] and millions of kids are mastering it by learning to slaughter bystanders,” Ted Koppel told America.

Nightline devoted 20 minutes of its broadcast to GTA in July 2002. It interviewed children who grinned ear to ear as they gunned down people in GTA, their parents who insisted it was just a game, a concerned expert who was sure GTA was training them to kill, and a psychologist who said that was bullshit. It all ended with a roundtable discussion where a police officer, in uniform, explained the differences between video games and real world violence.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas — Congressional Hearings and Sex on TV

I was an assistant manager of a Gamestop in Texas in 2004 when Rockstar released Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. The level of parental concern in the store was high in the weeks leading up to its release. One mother was so upset by a bearing a cover story about that she told me I was going to hell for “selling a gangster lifestyle” to children.

But it was sex, not violence, that the news focused on with . The game had a lot of simulation elements — its protagonist would gain weight if he ate too much — and Rockstar had experimented with a sex minigame called “hot coffee.” Developers cut the minigame from the final release, but it was still on the physical discs that went to stores. Modders uncovered it in the files and were able to patch it back in.

California politician Leland Yee got wind of the mod and condemned the Entertainment Software Ratings Board (ESRB) for labeling the game “Mature” instead of “Adults Only.” Cable news went wild. Rachel Maddow weighed in. Hillary Clinton, then a Senator in New York, demanded an investigation. Congress voted to send the FTC after Rockstar for deceiving the ESRB. 

The ESRB updated the game’s rating to an AO. Walmart, Best Buy, and other retailers . publisher Take-Two shipped new copies with the content completely removed. Take-Two’s shareholders also removed most of its board and put Strauss Zelnick in charge. He’s been the CEO ever since.

— The Ballad of Jack Thompson

The cultural winds had shifted by the time hit stores in 2008. Retailers across the country had midnight release parties where people lined up to purchase the game as soon as possible. Local news outlets interviewed people in line and marveled at how much money might make.

But the culture warriors still pointed to GTA as proof of America’s moral decline. Glenn Beck, then an anchor on CNN Headline News, on the game and often spoke to American lawyer Jack Thompson. Thompson hated Grand Theft Auto so much and was so sure it was training young people to kill their elders that he let his crusade against the franchise ruin his life.

Thompson against Take-Two aimed at preventing the company from selling at all. The publisher counter-sued, Thompson accused it of perjury, and the parties eventually settled. In its ruling, the courts said Thompson could never use the legal system to stop Take-Two from publishing a game ever again.

He didn’t stop though. After the game came out, Thompson Rockstar had based an assassination mission on him. He then sent a letter to Strauss Zelnick’s mom. “Your son, this very moment, is doing everything he possibly can to sell as many copies of GTA IV to teen boys in the United States, a country in which your son claims you raised him to be ‘a Boy Scout.’ More like the Hitler Youth, I would say. Happy Mother’s day, Mrs. Zelnick, which this year is May 11, two weeks after your son unleashes porn and violence upon other mothers’ boys. I'm sure you’re very proud,” Thompson wrote in the letter.

The Supreme Court of Florida permanently disbarred him shortly thereafter.

Money in the Age of Violence

In 2013, made a billion dollars in three days and was the biggest entertainment release of all time. It made more money than any movie, book, album, or video game had ever made before. Every news broadcast about the game led with that fact. “Never has there been an opening like this in the entertainment industry,” CBS News said.

Jake Tapper and CNET’s Dan Ackerman lamented that GTA V’s success would hurt the creativity of the video game industry. “It’s become such a hit-driven business. You have to have a big opening day or opening weekend for anyone to take you seriously. And when you have such a hit-driven business, I think people get risk averse and they don’t get as creative,” Ackerman told Tapper. 

The news still ran segments about the violence and sex in the game, but it was typically couched in a conversation about its runaway financial success. Most anchors brought on experts who told them about the business. They sought to understand what was happening and why people liked the game, rather than condemning it outright. 

Anxieties of American Decline

In 2026, cultural fears about violence and sex in video games are gone. Instead, we’re all worried about money. Everyone is sure will make money, the question is if it will make the money?

“Why the stakes for GTA VI are so high,” declared the thumbnail for a Bloomberg video about the game. The outlet’s podcast also ran an episode about why the . Newsweek worried that the U.S. economy as people take time off work to play. CBS News’ morning show wondered how much money the game would make and the anchor admitted he once “lost a summer” to Grand Theft Auto. No one discussed violence at all. CNBC’s coverage called the game a “Billion Dollar Hype Machine.”

Behind it all is a kind of lament — a worry that might be a final hurrah for this kind of game. Rumors are that it cost a billion dollars. Games are more expensive than ever and the industry has been devastated. A third of the industry lost their jobs in the past 24 months and most of them . Even when a game is successful, companies cut staff. wondered if GTA VI “may be the last great heist.”

Underneath all these economic fears, the older panics still lurked. On Fox News, middling collegiate swimmer turned political activist Riley Gaines hoped that the game’s romantic elements would lead to a rise in birth rates. “Hopefully these men realize they like the feeling of love, romantic love, and go out and find it. Because, I’ll tell you what, we’re in a population decline. We need more babies. You can’t have babies, real babies, mouths to feed, from video games,” Gaines said.

Twitch streamer Sasha Grey had early access to the game and was streaming it to YouTube and Twitch when YouTube shut down her stream for “nudity.” An early cutscene showed what Grey described as “artistic nip and some booty.” Grey complained to YouTube in a post on X and shared a screenshot of the moment the company shut down her stream. 

“They allow far worse under their educational category. This game is art, y’know? It’s the biggest release of the friggin’ decade,” Grey said during her stream. She pulled up the post on X to see if she’d gotten a response. “Oh god, the Twitter post got labeled as adult content, which means it’s going to be harder to get seen.”

The old protestant advertiser-friendly anti-sex morality is still there, programmed into the computer systems we use every day.

items.title: Broken World
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
Very chonky newsletter today as we have published quite a lot over the last 24 hours. Today we look into why everything is busted and have an extremely wild story about how people are using their AI agents.

A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay, a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging.

Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. Over the weekend, people who I do not normally talk to about my job asked me: What is going on with the airplanes? Why is my bank down? What about Microsoft?

The default assumption that many people are making is that these are either being caused by cyberattacks and/or “AI” broadly defined, whether that’s AI gone haywire, “rogue” AI agents, or something else, which is indicative of just how fearful people are of AI. What I have been telling people is, basically, that shit is broken and things are going to keep breaking. For lots of different reasons. It’s often not a hack and it’s often not explicitly AI-related, but everything now sort of looks like that XKCD comic of the dependency domino tower.

While not exactly true that AI and cyberattacks are causing these outages, it’s also not entirely wrong, either. What we’re seeing is — I think — a series of infrastructure failures (and some cyberattacks) that are not directly connected but are broadly a symptom of the same general trends and systemic problems we’ve seen across society, the government, and the tech sector over the last several years.

First, it’s worth mentioning that anytime there’s a string of outages, there’s a tendency to tie them altogether. And outages or hacks that previously wouldn’t have been noted at all suddenly get more attention and become part of the narrative. Take, for example, the fact that the International Ice Hockey Federation has been targeted by a cyberattack; you probably would not normally hear about this but it has suddenly become part of the broader story.

The simplest explanation I can come up with for the broader disastrous trend we’ve seen is that since the pandemic we have seen:

  • mass layoffs of tech workers and software developers
  • mass deployment of AI-assisted and vibe coded products, software updates, and patches
  • mass layoffs in the government sector and outright destruction of government expertise and oversight
  • the loss of institutional knowledge associated with those layoffs and funding cuts
  • a failure to invest in upgrading infrastructure/redundancy
  • government contracts handed out to the President’s friends and political allies
  • AI and LLM-assisted/iterative exploit discovery, coding, and deployment
  • companies responding to the AI hacking threat with AI-coded and rushed patches

When Elon Musk took over Twitter and named it X, there were many people who thought his layoffs and the associated loss of expertise would result in the site failing basically because of an infrastructural failure. Twitter would basically “go down” because someone would break something and no one would know how to fix it. We haven’t really seen that happen to X, but that same philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government.

Use code 404MEDIA

A man and his Muse sue MetaA little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Joe Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”

The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful. See more of my extremely bizarre trip down this rabbit hole here.

On the podcast this week, Joseph talks about his investigation into OnlyFakes, the AI-powered fake ID service.

And part two of the podcast features my call with Joe Thomas, who is using his Muse agent to sue the company that made it.

A new Gallup poll shows that 33 percent of young people they polled between the ages of 15 and 22 have an AI companion.

A reminder that we have new merch in stock. 404 ‘Doom Code’ short sleeve t-shirts and trucker hats. We’ve heard from some of you about wanting new designs/different cuts, etc. Promise we are doing a bigger refresh of our merch store as soon as we possibly can. Just waiting on designs and trying to manage how we do fulfillment.

Our friends over at Hell Gate are doing a sale. Get 25 percent off an annual subscription a t-shirt. We share notes on running a business with Hell Gate all the time and they’ve become some of our closest friends in the biz, so check them out, especially if you live in NYC. Even as someone who lives across the country, I find my subscription to be easily worth it.

The first reviews of are out and people are pretty unanimously saying it’s a masterpiece. This is, obviously, the video game event of … the decade? The millennium so far? I have not played any of them since GTA II so I will abstain from embarrassing myself further, but I trust Jason Schreier and he says it’s very good and possibly tech populist in vibe.

BugMeNot, a website where people shared logins to sites that shouldn’t have had logins, has suddenly disappeared without explanation after roughly two decades online. Bummer.

Voyager I is now one light day away from Earth. TIL that Voyager I launched a week Voyager 2 and Voyager 2 will not be a light day away from Earth for another decade. Space.com has a good writeup of why this is the case.

items.title: Massive New Study Shows How Young People Feel About AI Companions
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.

Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.

The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”

People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.

They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”

Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”

The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.

“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, , and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”

The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.

“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.
