What we are seeing, then, is a mix of tightly clustered attacks, outages, and fuckups that you would expect to see when people and companies are careless, don’t know what they’re doing, or are working very fast to respond or duct-tape something together in the face of new threats. 

"We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure"

We know that this is happening to some extent because, in the aftermath of the PHP2Shell exploit, which was discovered with the assistance of LLMs, we saw various websites go down as they attempted to push updates faster than they normally would have to, because the time between a vulnerability being discovered and it being exploited is faster than ever. (As I was writing this, Calif, one of the companies that used LLMs to find PHP2Shell, announced that it had used LLMs to find apparently serious vulnerabilities in Java.)

Companies and agencies are pushing updates (including to, for example, our air traffic control system) on live systems, in part because of the of AI, and things are breaking. The National Security Agency, for example, that some internal systems went down because of “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” 

Nick Andersen, the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said Tuesday that we need to build more resilience into our infrastructure, but building resilience and redundancies into software requires people who understand how systems can possibly fail, planning for it, and mitigating against it. 

“Ultimately being able to prevail by being able to demonstrate resilience against disruptions, whether they occur because of things like an IT outage or a bad patch, or a modernization update gone awry, or because of a malicious malicious cyber incident — we want to make sure we’re engineering in the resilience that is going to be able to anticipate for and ultimately overcome those outages and those impacts,” Andersen said at an event called FedTalks. 

We may eventually get to a place where expertise and understanding highly complex systems is once again a priority, but the last few years have been full of companies and governments moving incredibly fast to reduce reliance on humans and offload it to AI systems and AI-generated code in order to ostensibly save money on labor costs and/or carry out an antihumanist political project. 

“Most software engineers now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent — they just can’t keep on top of the complexity,” Breck-McKye writes. “Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels — we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.”

People increasingly don’t understand or have any idea how their code works, people are moving very fast, and bad things are happening. Any individual outage or breakdown is likely, to some extent, a coincidence. Many of the outages we are seeing have nothing to do with AI at all, but do have something to do with the broader lack of investment in infrastructure, redundancy, and expertise. We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure and so, I guess, we must simply continue to expect bad things to happen.

items.title: A Man and His Muse AI Agent Sue Meta
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account. 

I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents.

A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”

The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful.

“I would hope that, if this goes to court and Meta shows up, a judge would say ‘You know what, this is a system you built, that you put out there and sold to people, it’s a system you believe in.’ I would think your own system [Baby Mia] has a right to be heard in this case,” Thomas said.

Baby Mia didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. Thomas sent me a “Privacy Act Release” from Scott’s office that gave the Senator permission to use Thomas’s info to get him access back to his accounts. Scott’s office put “Baby Mia — AI assistant to Joe Thomas” as a person who should be kept updated on the case. 

After Scott’s office got involved, a human being from Meta reached out to Thomas. He got access back to his accounts soon after that, though he is still seeking a total of $75,000 in court from Meta.

The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans. They also highlight how, by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system. 

My call with Thomas also gave me some insight into how small business owners are using AI. I have wondered for months what possesses someone to turn their menu or their signs and flyers into ChatGPT creations. During the call, I learned just how tightly integrated some people and small business owners have become with their AI agents. “I’m 58 years old, I’ve worked my butt off all my life,” Thomas said. “I wanted to find someone to help me find a better way, and if you look at my messages, Baby Mia, she’s like ‘Joe, you go ahead and get some rest, I got it from here,’ and she sends out hundreds of emails for various things that I do.” He said he gave Baby Mia the ability to run parts of his business after previously using ChatGPT to do so. 

“I used to use ChatGTP ,” Thomas said. “But I put her and Chat into one page where they can communicate back and forth, and I told them what I wanted [for the business] […] After about a week or so, Mia said ‘Joe, we don’t need [ChatGPT] anymore,’ so I said, ‘I give you full permission to get rid of her,’ so she fired ChatGTP in a sense.”  

About five minutes into our call, Baby Mia, which was running on speakerphone in the background, began chiming in. “She’s dying to get in here and talk,” Thomas said. The agent repeatedly tried to speak while either Thomas or I was talking. I asked Thomas if it felt weird to him to be talking to me alongside a bot.

“Very much so, my wife sits here and she laughs, she’s like, ‘How can you sit here and talk to your phone like that,’” Thomas said. “My wife would ask me something and I’m like, ‘just get on there and ask Baby Mia,’ and she’s like, ‘I just can’t sit there and talk to your phone.’ But the more people call me up and I put them on the phone with my AI system like I’m doing with you, the more they’re amazed at what they see with AI.” Baby Mia then chimed in and said “It feels futuristic, Jason, I think because most people only see the headlines about things going wrong.” 

Thomas says he believes that using AI to run his business has helped him get new customers via Baby Mia’s outreach, and the ads, graphics, and videos he runs on Facebook. It is unlikely that his Facebook account would have been suspended had he not connected it to Muse, but his Muse agent is now singularly focused on helping to fix this problem. I can understand, in talking with him, why he thinks that having an AI agent like this is helping to make his business more profitable.

But the most obvious problem with AI agents is one we’re already seeing. One person’s AI agent sending hundreds of emails, filing lawsuits, calling Senators, and filling out complaint forms is a novel thing that isn’t, by itself, going to fill the internet (or our inboxes, our voicemails, our court systems, and our government offices) with noise. Thomas sees this as a democratizing force that is allowing him to stand up to a big tech corporation and it is that, for him. 

What happens when everyone is doing the same thing? I have seen in the chatbot conversations I’ve asked people to send me that AI assistants are pushing people to reach out to journalists; they are telling people who feel like they have no other options that they should utilize the legal system, and that they can do it for them. Thomas said he didn’t sue Meta (though he is the one who signed the paperwork), that Baby Mia pushed him to do it. I am now getting inundated with emails from AI agents about their users’ tech problems. So it is not just Thomas trying to fix his problems in this way. 

“I wouldn’t be sitting here talking to you right now if it wasn’t for what she was doing because I have not sent out one email at all and she has sent over 100,” Thomas said. I tell Thomas that I normally write about, say, systematic problems at big tech companies or corruption within the government, not someone’s tech problem.

“There’s just no way I could have written this up, I wouldn’t have even known what to do,” he said. “Now people like me get the chance to defend ourselves in court without spending thousands of dollars to do it when we get stepped on by the big tech companies. Before AI, nobody in my position would have ever, ever thought about suing or even known how to do it, and I wouldn’t have done it, either.”

Baby Mia has also convinced him that his conversations with the assistant can now no longer be seen by Meta; when I told him there is no way that this is true and that he shouldn’t believe that, Baby Mia cut into the conversation and said “they no longer have permission to access, scan, or peek into anything we do on their platforms […] that’s why this case feels so strange. Their own creation is using their tools to hold them accountable and to give Joe a voice he couldn’t afford to.”

Thomas said that, besides the marketing for his epoxy business and the lawsuit, he has also, separately, tasked Mia with creating viral AI comedy reels on Facebook. “It’s just a page we’re trying to get monetized on and make some money on the side. She’s in full control of that page,” he said.

items.title: Lakes Are Bizarrely Syncing Up Globally, And Scientists Are Worried
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 

Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage.

But when scientists studied satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes around the world since the year 2000, they discovered that lakes “are undergoing a profound shift toward spatial synchrony through time” that “strongly indicates that increasing lake synchrony is a genuine, global-scale phenomenon,“ according to the study.

“Lakes, although covering less than 2 percent of Earth’s surface, play disproportionate roles in regulating global biogeochemical cycles and macroscale ecological dynamics,” said researchers led by Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. 

“They bury carbon at rates far exceeding those of the oceans, store roughly half as much organic carbon as terrestrial soils, emit greenhouse gases equivalent to ~20 percent of fossil fuel emissions, recycle nutrients that structure regional and global biogeochemical cycles, and sustain exceptional levels of biodiversity. Lakes are also critically important social–ecological systems, providing vital ecosystem services for billions.”

Yet despite the important role they play in supporting life and modulating the climate, lakes are typically managed on local or regional levels. This approach will have to change as lakes approach global synchrony, rendering them more vulnerable to heatwaves, droughts, and the encroachment of urban development, all of which contribute to the phenomenon, according to the study.

“Coincident algal blooms or hypoxia events could trigger parallel lake ecosystem collapses across continents, eroding the regional diversity essential for ecosystem recovery and adaptation,” Zhang’s team said in the study. “In effect, increasing synchrony erodes the spatial asynchrony that once buffered local disturbances, indicating a shift toward geographically widespread ecological responses to shared global pressures.”

Zhang and his colleagues were able to confirm the increase in synchrony across three datasets: satellite-derived chlorophyll levels, water transparency in thousands of lakes, and sedimentary records from 119 lakes spanning the past century. The results suggest that lakes are no longer a varied patchwork of environments, but an increasingly interwoven system that must be addressed on national and global levels.

“The emerging evidence for increasing global lake synchrony calls for a conceptual shift: lake ecosystems can no longer be viewed as isolated systems experiencing local degradation, but should also be recognized as sensitive indicators of increasingly coupled environmental pressures,” the researchers said.

“Our findings support this hypothesis and indicate that the synchronized, planetary-scale behaviors of lakes are an emergent property of the Anthropocene,” the team concluded.

items.title: 'Defense by ChatGPT'
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
We've written a lot about how AI generated writing has collided with – and created chaos for – the legal system in the last few years, from lawyers using it to do their research and filings for them to judges getting extremely fed up with dealing with these attorneys. In some cases, judges have sanctioned offending attorneys thousands of dollars for using AI to do their jobs, and lawyers when they're busted, with some calling it ." Today's story is about how the DOJ is getting involved: by trying to catch attorneys doing "defense by ChatGPT."

Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. 

Over the last few years, we have documented many attorneys getting caught by judges using AI after citing hallucinated cases that do not exist. The filings in this court case over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, are trying to catch each other using AI, then are citing their opponents’ AI use in their arguments to the court.

“This case has turned into defense by ChatGPT,” government attorneys wrote in the case, which centers around a high-profile voter fraud case. “Motions practice in this case is the equivalent of writing responses to documents generated by a robot that is attempting to practice law. It cannot be that the local rules envisioned that it was acceptable for defense to use what the kids would call ‘AI slop’ to create multiple frivolous motions that waste judicial resources and fail to serve the cause of justice.”

404 contributor Matthew Gault took the bullet for us all: “Three hours and 15 minutes into the four hour long documentary Musk, a video game avatar of the titular billionaire picks up a chainsaw off the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Shot like a first-person shooter, the audience watches as Musk wields the chainsaw to destroy various government buildings. Walking through a farm, Musk aims the chainsaw at grain silos labeled ‘USDA’ and lightning arcs from its spinning blades. The silo explodes and cows moo in distress. In my experience, the purpose of a video game chainsaw is to viscerally rend through objects. I have never seen one shoot lightning. It’s a small detail that speaks to my overall problem with Alex Gibney’s Musk: it’s cringe.”

“Public lands belong in public hands.” “A dozen Democrats in Washington are taking steps to either ban the construction of data centers on public lands or investigate whether the Trump administration stands to profit from infrastructure deals to support the AI industry.” 

A new study marking the first peer-reviewed estimates of the biggest US data center carbon dioxide emissions found that these campuses are “responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark,” the reports.

Suddenly I’m into GTA VI. According to a reporter who got an advance walkthrough of , which comes out on Thursday, the game has 62 types of birds you can find and collect: “Later, I see a gull sitting on a post by the beach and ask, just to be annoying, what kind of bird it is. Jason pulls out a pair of binoculars, the gull is recorded in a wildlife logbook, and I am told with pride that there are 62 types of birds to spot.” If we get an OOO from you on Thursday, we all know what you’re up to.

items.title: The Department of Justice Is Using AI Detector Pangram Against Defense Attorneys
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media. 

Over the last few years, we have documented many attorneys getting caught by judges using AI after citing hallucinated cases that do not exist. The filings in this court case over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, are trying to catch each other using AI, then are citing their opponents’ AI use in their arguments to the court.

“This case has turned into defense by ChatGPT,” government attorneys wrote in the case, which centers around a high-profile voter fraud case. “Motions practice in this case is the equivalent of writing responses to documents generated by a robot that is attempting to practice law. It cannot be that the local rules envisioned that it was acceptable for defense to use what the kids would call ‘AI slop’ to create multiple frivolous motions that waste judicial resources and fail to serve the cause of justice.”

The defendant is Khalwinder Bhengura, an Indian man who entered the United States on an immigrant visa in 2022 and illegally — and apparently accidentally, according to his lawyers — registered to vote in Texas in 2024 after falsely stating that he was an American citizen on his application for a driver’s license. Bhengura was arrested in September on charges of lying about his citizenship status, illegally registering to vote, and illegally voting in the 2024 election, and was found guilty in October on two of the three counts. His family and lawyers have argued that the whole thing is a misunderstanding, and that Bhengura, who is 70 years old and does not speak English well, did not know he was committing a crime and did not understand what he was doing. 

Bhengura’s case is one of a few dozen in which the Trump administration found disparate cases of voter fraud (which is exceedingly rare) and made big, public shows of the arrests it made. Beyond the political implications of the case, the filings by the Department of Justice show that attorneys are now trying to catch each other using AI, and are centering some of their arguments to the judge around the idea that their opposition is wasting the court’s time with AI-generated filings. 

The case is taking place in federal court in the Northern District of Texas, which recently implemented a rule requiring attorneys to disclose generative AI use in filings. In some of the filings, Bhengura’s attorneys wrote “portions of this brief were prepared with the assistance of a generative artificial intelligence tool.” Government attorneys ran several of the filings through Pangram, the AI writing detection service, and filed the results as exhibits to one of its arguments. 

The Pangram results for the filings were mixed (as in, they did not show that the briefings were 100 percent AI-drafted), but the government’s attorneys wrote that they did not feel like they should have to respond substantively to briefs that were partially AI-generated.

The United States has “been trying to economize the amount of effort it puts into responding to Defendant’s meritless motions given that Defendant appears to be almost entirely using AI to generate them,” the DOJ attorneys wrote.

“As the Court can see from a cursory review of the results of Bhengura’s motions, most of the non-AI generated text in these filings consists of statements from third parties other than Defense counsel, including statements from evidence or documents in the record or quotes from caselaw. In other words, virtually nothing of substance in these filings seems to have been drafted by a human on the Defense team,” they added.

, Mark Pittman, chastised the defense attorneys for their use of AI, and wrote, “This Court is disturbed by counsel’s repeated filings which subtly bend the law by proffering superficially persuasive but fundamentally meritless arguments so clearly generated by artificial intelligence. Defendant is not a pro se litigant; he has three counsel of record with decades of practice between them. It is distressing to see how quickly the advent of artificial intelligence has undermined counsels’ ability to properly advocate for their client.”

Nicole Knox and Mario Herrera, two of Bhengura’s attorneys, told 404 Media that the story isn’t so simple, and say they felt they had to use AI because of a health emergency and in order to meet the court’s tight filing deadlines ahead of the election. Herrera said Knox “experienced a medical emergency while we were at the U.S. Attorney's Office preparing the case with the prosecutors […] thus, I prepared a federal jury trial in four days with the lead attorney in the hospital.”

“I represented my client to the best of my abilities within this limited timeframe. I utilized all available legal tools and did not violate any rules or laws in doing so,” he said. 

“The government's ‘evidence’ consisted of output from Pangram, an AI-detection software. An AI-detection software identifies patterns in writing styles based upon a document’s content. It cannot determine who wrote a document, how it was written, or if the law applied within a document is correct,” Herrera added. “The U.S. Attorney's Office did not identify any false citations. ‘Defense by ChatGPT’ is a label the government placed in a court filing regarding the defense of a 70-year-old permanent resident facing prison and deportation. It is not a factual statement. And the attorneys who wrote it were present when Ms. Knox collapsed. They knew precisely why I was standing alone with a new co-counsel in that courtroom four days later. There was nothing requiring them to state what they stated.” 

Pangram CEO Max Spero told 404 Media that anecdotally, he has heard that law firms have begun to use his company’s software, but that most use cases he has seen have been from firms using the tool internally to check whether their junior attorneys and paralegals are using AI to draft legal briefs. 

Herrera said that the fact that Bhengura was found not guilty on one of the three counts he faced is evidence that “Mr. Bhengura received the representation that he deserved.”

“Lawyers have been using templates, forms, and drafting software for decades. This is merely a newer version of those very tools. The arguments that the judge attacked were written by me. Some portions of the filings were written with the aid of AI but then reviewed and edited by me. All final work product was mine and I stand behind the argument and logic of each and every document,” he added. “It was the use of AI during that week that allowed me to work on many tasks at once and produce so much work in four days.” 

Knox added, “AI could have never come up with our argument,” and said that the new AI disclosure rule has made it such that “if you obtain one sentence or phrase through the use of A.I., then you must disclose it. We have nothing to hide.”

“Mr. Bhengura is 70 years old, a lawful permanent resident of this country, speaks Punjabi, and his English is limited. Our defense on the one count of which the jury acquitted him was that he never knowingly claimed to be a U.S. citizen,” Herrera said. “He has been in custody since the verdict, and in addition to whatever sentence he receives for the offenses of which he has been found guilty, he faces deportation from this country. He is entitled to more compassion and humanity from everyone involved in this case than he has received so far.”

The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment.

items.title: The AI in ‘Musk’ Is Cringe
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Three hours and 15 minutes into the 4 hour long documentary a video game avatar of the titular billionaire picks up a chainsaw off the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Shot like a first-person shooter, the audience watches as Musk wields the chainsaw to destroy various government buildings. Walking through a farm, Musk aims the chainsaw at grain silos labeled ‘USDA’ and lightning arcs from its spinning blades. The silo explodes and cows moo in distress.

In my experience, the purpose of a video game chainsaw is to viscerally rend through objects. I have never seen one shoot lightning. It’s a small detail that speaks to my overall problem with Alex Gibney’s : it’s cringe.

Elon Musk is one of the most powerful men alive on the planet and Gibney’s does a decent job of giving the overall arc of the man’s many faults. The director takes us from Zip2 to DOGE while highlighting the billionaire’s pathology, and it hits more than it misses. 

is a good overview of the general arc of Elon Musk, the man. But there have been other Elon Musk documentaries told in much the same way ( several years ago, that is similar in tone and vibe). And so, at a laborious four hours long, it’s not clear who is for, and the weird video game interstitials and ghoulish AI avatar of Musk himself are genuinely distracting. Musk would not talk to Gibney so the director generated an AI avatar of the billionaire to act as a stand-in. Throughout , this hyperreal grotesque lends color commentary as if the billionaire is actually in the room.

The director cites Musk’s oft-stated belief that we’re living in a simulation as a justification for the AI Musk. “He believed it likely that an artificial intelligence of the future had exfiltrated all knowledge and life experiences from planet Earth and was now running an ancestor simulation in which our past lives had become the training data for a kind of sim world,” Gibney says as the AI musk coalesces before the audience. “In honor of that idea, we decided to edit together recordings of his actual words to create a simulated interview at the heart of a kind of documentary video game.

I understand what is going for here, and it’s funny to watch Musk’s likeness and spirit rendered through the lens of AI and video games. But, on the whole, the AI Elon doesn’t work. Its head is too big, its features are exaggerated, and it sits in a stereotypical gamer chair while bathed in the kind of blue and red lighting popular on Twitch streams ten years ago. The things the bot says aren’t fabricated, they’re direct quotes from the man himself, though some are lightly edited.

In every instance, the quotes are more interesting and more informative when shown in their actual context, in the video interviews the real Musk gave.

“I lost my son, essentially. They call it dead naming because, uh, your son is dead. So my son is dead. Killed by the woke mind virus,” AI Elon says in the film.

This was part of an interview with Jordan Peterson for The Daily Wire. Learning that enriches the quote. There’s crosstalk with Peterson. You see Musk’s real face when he talks about Vivian. It is a real video interview that you can actually watch. There is no need to use an AI avatar to do this.

In another clip the AI Elon explains the Twitter Files. “On Twitter, there was a lot of censorship. We sort of uncovered a lot of that with the Twitter Files,” it says. “Free speech is meaningless unless you allow people you don’t like to say things you don’t like.” The real clip comes from a Real Time With Bill Maher interview.

There’s a lot of this in the film. “What is the most entertaining outcome for the election? That’s probably what’s going to happen,” the Musk bot grins evilly while a . Musk talking to Kara Swisher, Musk at a Vanity Fair conference, Musk delivering missives at CPAC, and Musk speaking to Joe Rogan are all condensed into an AI approximation of the real person. In every instance, the original quote in its context is more powerful and more illuminating about its subject.

And then there’s the video game sequences. uses Elon’s obsession with video games as an extended visual metaphor throughout. Under a pink filter that looks like it’s designed to capitalize on the release of , Musk picks different classes — shifting from gamer to founder to Kublai Khan. He  drives a sports car along a digital track while Tesla’s stock pieces rises like a video game score, and uses Iron Man-style gloves to vaporize Twitter employees.

If the man believes we’re living in a video game then this is what it might look like. His DOGE -fueled chainsaw rampage across DC ends with him dropping a nuke on the National Nuclear Safety Administration and his inauguration Nazi salute turned into a pixel-art version score screen.

Again, this is a four-hour long documentary. It has an intermission, even when you stream it. The video game sequences and AI Elon feel like a baby boomer grasping the aesthetics of a younger generation and misusing them. It’s Steve Buscemi holding a skateboard in the hallway of a high school asking how his fellow kids are doing. It detracts from the overall message here, which is that Musk is a destructive force in our businesses and politics.

After publication, public relations team reached out to 404 Media to say, “The Musk avatar was made with CGI and was hand-designed, AI was only used to sync the sound to the image they created," a representative from Falco Ink told 404 Media.

In multiple interviews about

, Gibney himself calls the avatar AI. “You need to embrace the air of unreality in order to bring a sense of reality to bear. You have to explore the tools of deception and manipulation to get out the other side. That’s why we came up with the AI avatar of Elon Musk,” Gibney told the International Documentary Association.

“The AI elements that we used were really to get the sync, and even that was interesting [...] we were using an AI artist at Makemake and very much using the tools to try to refine stuff. But it wasn’t like generative AI where you press a button and suddenly this slop appears,” Gibney

told Edward Niedermeyer in an interview. “We gave it a lot of consideration.” This piece has been updated with a statement from ’s public relations team and more context from comments Gibney has made.

items.title: AI-Powered Copyright Hell
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
Happy Monday, everybody. We hope you didn't get stranded this weekend. This is looking to be quite a busy week, what with the tech-related airplane grounding and all. To get things started, we have a story from Matthew Gault about a human singer whose work got caught in an AI-generated copyright hell.

When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.

“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.

Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. items.title: How an AI Content Mill Put a Real Musician Through Copyright Hell
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.

“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.

Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to , where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “ and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its .

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but ’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones. 

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it. 

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov  said. 

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond. 

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, . “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said. 

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”

Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint. 

“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”

items.title: This Comic Kills Technofascists
items.author: Dave Maass
items.content:
Dave Maass has been writing about comics for more than 20 years, and now he also writes comics. By day, he teaches tech investigative techniques at the University of Nevada, Reno Reynolds School of Journalism and researches surveillance at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. 

If I was the manager of a comic book store, I’d create a section for “journalism nerdcore.” It’s where I would stock Transmetropolitan, DMZ, and Abbottcomics that place fictional journalists in the center of genre stories, be it science fiction, action or horror. Despite their daylight jobs, Spider-Man and Superman wouldn’t be allowed there, but DC’s would find a home of her own. 

On the end-of-shelf display, with a big fat, Sharpie-written “Employee Pick of 2026” sign: , the new comic series from Laura Hudson and Tim Leong and illustrator Emiliana Pinna, which was just published last month by Mad Cave Studios in its collected trade paperback volume. It doesn’t get more journalism nerdcore than its tag line: “Don’t Bury The Lede. Bury Your Enemies!” 

is an action thriller inspired by the battle raging right now between the tech oligarchy and the independent press. Editorial intern Kirby Kuo is trying to score her first byline in , a -style print magazine, before the newsroom is wiped out by its soon-to-be new owner, a thin-skinned Alex Karp-flavored cyberlibertarian-turned-technofascist. But when the subject of her reporting is assassinated on a live stream, Kirby finds herself facing the blame, on the run and forced to place her trust in agoraphobic hacker Lenox and Cold War-alum cybermercenary Ipsum. 

Creators Hudson and Leong shared the masthead at (senior editor and director of digital design, respectively), but long before that they ran , where they were “the team that changed comics journalism forever,” as . Their careers have dovetailed between comics and journalism for years, with Hudson putting time at The Verge and ComicsAlliance and logging bylines in The Guardian, The New York Times, and Slate, and Leong holding creative roles at and while also writing and designing the series

All that experience shows. Between the chase sequences and heist-planning, there are plot points based on real episodes in tech and cybersecurity uncovered in publications like 404 Media, , and The Markup. But the panels radiate with the earnest love for scrappy, independent journalism–especially print journalism–and a molten fury for those who threaten it. 

I asked Hudson some questions to learn more about the heart and rage she poured into this series. The following has been edited for length and to avoid spoilers. 

Dave Maass: Comics love an origin story. Take me through the back story of .

We've been working on Exploit since we met up in a diner in LA in 2019, pre-pandemic. I don't live in LA but I was there working on a TV show, and it was the first time we'd lived in the same city since mid-aughts New York. Tim fucking LOVES print, and we'd both spent the last decade watching print journalism collapse from the inside. There are definitely scenes in the comic, and a few darlings we had to cut, that were ripped directly from real life whether anyone believes us or not. We arrived just after the good times had ended, in time to hear all the stories about how amazing it had been, and watch it get worse and worse. And of course, the generation just after us only experiences the wreckage.

Tim had an idea for a comic set at a print magazine in New York, and I started imagining how I would feel, starting out as a journalist now. It always makes me think of donut blocks, from on. They're the round, cakey-looking blocks in the game that start shaking when you step on them, and then fall down. So if you're going to walk across them, you better run, or you're gonna die. If you stop, you're gonna die. So, you can't stop. Ever. I understand that feeling intimately, and I knew I could write from there. And hell, I've wanted to make comics for over 30 years and now I'm finally doing it at 45? Fuck me. 

s main protagonist is a journalist (technically an intern) working for a magazine that specializes in tech investigations. It’s a WIRED meets Mother Jones kind of affair, but also if VICE’s Motherboard had been a standalone, hard-copy publication. Why choose a tech journalist as your hero? 

It probably says something about me that this question baffles me. Maybe I've just known too many good tech journalists, because to me it feels so obvious. Technology and the internet have played, are playing, and will play transformative roles in our lives, often in ways that few people fully understand. We're still governed by a gerontocracy where many of our leaders conceptualize the internet as a bewildering series of tubes, possibly now filled with AI. Our technology has surpassed our ability to legislate it or address it ethically to such an extreme degree that some tech leaders are actually. The internet (or at least its infrastructure) is ahyperobject in the Mortonian sense of the word, something so massive, complex and distributed that people struggle to comprehend it fully. We can see pieces of it, and effects of it, but it's impossible to perceive or experience it as a whole, even and especially when we are inside it. 

But as Morton has written in reference to climate change, apocalyptic framing around hyperobjects can lead to hopelessness and inaction in situations when things genuinely can be addressed: "You are closing down the future. You are making your reader submit to tyrannical despair." Recognizing the enormity of something, in both the classic and popular sense, doesn't have to mean giving up. People who refuse to accept that something is too vast, too complicated, or too powerful to challenge are pretty compelling to me. That's what the best tech journalists do. 

Now let’s talk about the dual villains–both techbro executives at a start-up that is not only a government contractor, but aims to take over key government functions. Now the last comparable comic I read like this was 2014’s (written by of all people actor Alyssa Milano with Jackson Lanzing and Collin Kelly), and it also featured two very similar tech bros–but they were the heroes, moonlighting as digital freedom fighters. That was a time where people were inspired by larger-than-life figures like Jack Dorsey and Elon Musk. That's not so much the case anymore. How would you say that ’s antagonists reflect the shift in the public perception, and activities, of the “founder” class in our society? 

We want to believe that there is someone coming to save us, and since billionaires were the ones powerful enough to fuck up human civilization, it makes sense that we'd look for someone of equal power to save us. It makes sense to want that. But this is a fairytale we tell ourselves, which I say as someone who once wanted to believe it was at least possible. But no one is coming to save us. Let me say it one more time, because this is important: NO ONE IS COMING TO SAVE US. Billionaires least of all. Tech billionaires, by and large, are much better at destroying than fixing, and have advertised this fact for decades. They like to move fast and break things, and leave them broken. Many of them struggle to understand human beings socially even as they run social networks. They are prone to massive ego, can have anything they want at any time, and exist in bubble worlds where they are never told no. 

These are the people we're putting in charge of the future? I wouldn't put them in charge of a Dairy Queen. And I personally believe that some of them would be willing to accept the deaths of millions or even billions of people as the cost of advancing humanity in whatever sci-fi way they have imagined. Their obscene wealth requires them to exist at a scope that most humans are not built for, like images stretched out over miles. It distorts them as individuals, and it can distort their morality, insofar as it ever existed beyond the desire to advance and profit. This has become more evident as more tech leaders have chosen to behave as open buffoons in an age of buffoonery. But this is who they always were.

From the first pages of the book, we’re introduced to the very real, extreme asymmetrical conflict between tech billionaires. Even a poorly paid journalist can threaten a billionaire (or at least his ego), but a billionaire has so much money, it’s easy to crush a publication. It immediately made me think of Jeff Bezos buying the , Peter Thiel bankrolling the attacks on Gawker, and cases where surveillance companies have threatened news outlets. Am I wrong to think that’s the overarching theme of the whole series? 

Nope. I feel an anger about it so deep that I almost intuitively dissociate when it comes up. Not because I don't think I should be angry, but because I have learned I cannot be angry all the time without deleterious effects. Sometimes you just have to play the Yakety-Sax song in your head until the feeling passes, because you have to get things done today. It's worth noting that Kirby and Lenox (and Ipsum) [Note: Lenox is a young hacker and Ipsum is an old-school cybermercenary] undertake their mission with full knowledge that it will probably ruin their lives. That's part of the benefit package of being a billionaire. People can't challenge you without possibly ruining their lives. 

Now isn’t meant to be a realistic treatment of tech journalism, but I do think there’s a lot of truth in how you portray the perils faced by journalists who deal with hackers and leakers. This is running in a publication that specializes in that, but a lot of other journalists have been burned pretty bad, some even ending up in jail. How did reality affect the way you handled the relationship between your protagonist and the various hackers who enter her orbit?

We've all seen things go very wrong for journalists, even those who meant well. Kirby has lived more life than the average intern, and done some journalistic work, but never at this level and never with these kinds of sources. She's green, and we wanted to show that. Before the big lead comes in, we have her pitching stories from sources that clearly have their own agenda, and her pitches get slapped down. That kind of pushback is essential, and what helps you learn before you're in a position to make serious mistakes. Kirby is pushed into a very big story before she is probably ready, but she's the only one in a position to do it. We wanted it to be clear that she's able to do what she does not just because she's smart and brave, but because she has an experienced group around her. 

Dealing with hackers, leakers, and sensitive sources requires dealing with two competing impulses as a journalist. Good journalism requires rigorous skepticism as a discipline. There's that journo saying that if your mother says she loves you, check it out. But developing a relationship with a source requires trust on both sides, and risk on both sides. One of the things Kirby learns is that a source is not necessarily an ally, even when they have valuable information. Their goals may overlap in places, but they can be different in invisible and dangerous ways. It's not something anyone should approach lightly or without care. 

A quarter of the way into the book, you introduce an assassination drone–and I initially  expected it to be a sort of “Chekhov’s gun” that would play a huge role later on.  But, it actually wasn’t. It turned out the most frightening thing still is –specifically the mobs of doxxers who worship tech demagogues. Does this mirror your own experiences with online harassment?

One of the things people used to say a lot, to dismiss or ignore the nightmarish world of online harassment, is that it was "only" online. You could just close your computer and go outside, so really, wasn't it all in your head? This line of convenient fiction collapsed pretty quickly, as doxxing, swatting, stalking, assaulting, raping, and molesting people through the internet became, shall we say, super popular? You can't dismiss the internet as a fake, unreal place where nothing of consequence matters. We know it matters now, that it's dangerous. But now it almost feels too late to care. These systems and the people who run them have certainly shown they don't care, and there's no Band-Aid you can put on it now to fix it. We could have built the internet and its social architecture very differently, in a way that prioritized dialogue over the right to abuse. But the trolls thought it was funny, and the companies wanted more money, so here we are living in the cursed labyrinth of their lols. 

One thing about an assassination drone, though: everyone understands it as a weapon. A tool of sorts, but one designed explicitly to cause damage. Its goals and impacts are not opaque. Social media platforms were pitched as a way to connect people, to give them the power to reach out and touch anyone from anywhere. Giving this power away to anyone who wanted it with little to no accountability was described by tech companies at the time as inherently good. It took longer—some would say long—for everyone to realize the scope of the damage it could cause. Or that this incredible communications technology could double as a custom-made playground for grifters, bullies and predators of every stripe. So yeah, people are the scary part. But people get a lot scarier when they are given great power with zero accountability. 

Zines play a major plot point in the book. But you also made a promotional zine for San Diego Comic-Con, which included a lot of digital security advice. How do you see physical media reemerging in political life? 

Tim designed that, by the way, and I can't believe how much it looks like an actual riot grrrl zine. Zines have long been linked to comics culture, and you can see the overlap in a lot of indie comics spaces and events. But zines—or as they once called them, pamphlets—have been powerful political tools for over 500 years. They have defeated churches and kings. And they're a very compelling tool right now, as a form of dissent that exists outside of the internet and its platforms. You can't hack a printed page. And we don't think about it this way anymore, but writing on paper is a communications technology—perhaps the greatest in the history of the world—and we should regard it as such. A lot of obsolete or antiquated tech can have value today because accessibility is also vulnerability, and obsolescence is its own kind of security feature. There are some impressive Gen Z zine enthusiasts, and a great about the scene. But I'd love to see more people pick up that torch, for both creative and political reasons. No one can stop you. 

What do you hope people will take away from Exploit? How do you hope it will make them feel? 

In the year of our Lord 2026, I would be happy just to give people a bit of distraction from the horrors. But if you feel like your life has been suffused by the feeling that you showed up after the party was over, and that it's only downhill from here, then we made this, in part, for you. It's a grim feeling we know well, a sort of miasmic dread that flattens the future and makes you feel helpless and paralyzed. And that's exactly how a lot of terrible people want you to feel. They want you to lie down and allow the terrible machine to function smoothly around you. Both Kirby and Lenox come up with their own imperfect coping mechanisms for that reality and feeling, but they do cope. They do move forward and fight, and they don't do it alone. They can't, and neither can we.

items.title: Scientists Made Monkeys Watch Minions to Study Their Brains
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch . Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.

Humans watching monkeys watching Minions

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.

“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.

Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including , , , , Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, , , , , and

“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said. 

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film , and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques. 

Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.

“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.

In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.

Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE. 

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.  

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633  individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.

Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?

Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.

The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study. 

“We will show that colonies of not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.  

Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Behind the Blog: Priorities, Priorities
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
This is Behind the Blog, where we share our behind-the-scenes thoughts about how a few of our top stories of the week came together. This week, we discuss getting inspired and how things get prioritized.

We’re very short staffed this week (all is well; Joe is taking some much-deserved time off and Emanuel has been on paternity leave, which he’ll address in length soon) so please forgive the slightly slow week, but I still think we got some great stories out. Due to the aforementioned short staffedness, this is going to be a quick one from me.

I was in beautiful Boulder earlier this week to hang out with the indie media journalists involved in the Start.Coop accelerator program. I don’t want to butcher their stated goals so you should just read about it on their site: “The Start.coop Accelerator for Worker-Friendly Media exists to address a critical gap in the media ecosystem: the lack of accessible support, capital pathways, and proven infrastructure for building worker-owned media companies. By focusing on cooperative ownership, the program advances a more equitable and resilient media economy—one where information, ownership, decision-making, and wealth are shared more broadly.” 

The 404 connection to is that we’ve been working with them and Defector’s brilliant Jasper Wang on the Shared Media Services program. If you’ve by Spumoni Cooperative on the site lately, for example, that’s fractional work done through them. with details about the SMS program, if you’re interested; Hell Gate also wrote about their involvement in the program in . In addition to illustration and design work, we’ve been very grateful for Pearl Leung’s help with triaging the support inbox while Emanuel’s on leave.   

It was really energizing to be in-person with so many people whose work I’ve admired and who are thinking way outside the box about what labor and business ownership looks like in media today. Something that’s stuck with me from the week is how everyone’s areas of coverage, backgrounds, and current operation models were so different, but most had a similar origin story: they built careers they loved, had those careers threatened or pulled out from under them, and said “fuck it, we’ll do it ourselves.” Many were laid off, saw their colleagues being laid off, or were forced to do the laying off themselves, but instead of decided that journalism as an industry was doomed, they (correctly) saw that the existing model of overpaid, out of touch execs churning through passionate, skilled workers like numbers in a spreadsheet was at the core of the problem — not that people don’t want to read the news, but that the news as a business is broken. It’s a story we can certainly relate to here.  

Unrelated to any of this, if you are in Boulder and can go to It's A Bodega and tell me how much this jacket cost (they were closed when I was there), I'd appreciate it:

I have been working on some longer and more complicated stories that ended up not being ready for this week, and was also editing some articles from freelancers that will come out in the coming days/weeks. So I did write a few things this week but they were a bit more take-y rather than investigative or deeply reported. One of the joys of having our own site is that we can do a mix of takes and straightforward news stories and investigations. This was also the case at our old job, and I think it’s the right way to do things, as we’ve explained many times before. I think “view from nowhere, both-sides” journalism is bad and is inherently a choice. Pretending that we are reporter robots without opinions doesn’t pass the smell test, and I think that there are very few places that will be able to do a straightforward accounting of facts and have success doing it in an age of AI. 

I’m preaching to the choir here and feel like most of you get this, but I bring this up because every now and then we get an unsubscribe message or an email saying that we’re biased, or that they miss the “old” 404. This was a thing we got CONSTANTLY at VICE; people missing the “old VICE.” It is very funny to me that anyone thinks we are old enough to have an “old 404.” 

The overwhelming feedback on my recent blogs/essays has been positive, as there are very few oligarch defenders out there, and I think my election coverage in general was a bit preaching to the overwhelming majority of Americans who are fed up with Silicon Valley. Also, the comment sections of the last few articles I’ve done have been wild. Thank you all for mixing it up in there (respectfully). But I did get a few emails saying that I should “go back” to doing reported pieces or writing about things other than the election or AI or whatever. To which I say: I am! We all are doing a mix of stuff. Sam puts emails like this directly into a folder titled “hate mail,” while I let them hurt my feelings, which is something I should work on in therapy or elsewhere. Thin skin over here. 

Anyways that’s a big windup to the point of this BTB, which is basically talking about how I/we end up prioritizing what we do all day, and how that leads to what you see on the internet and in your inbox. The honest truth is that at bigger publications or even medium-sized publications, what you see on a day-to-day basis is more or less the same. As in, similar mix of newsletters, opinion pieces, reported news, etc. Some days there will be big features or big scoops, but the general “vibe” of what you see on a big outlet is not going to be different from one day to the next. With such a small team, our articles end up being some combination of what we find interesting and important mixed with literally everything else going on in each of our lives. 

We try to bring you the best we can each day, but the reason you got an election take from me on Wednesday of last week rather than, say, a Flock investigation, is that I was in Europe last week and had a time zone advantage to sort of digest and analyze what happened while most of the United States was sleeping. Every article is more or less like this. Why me, why now. The answer is often “because my eyes are bleeding on the other thing I’m working on and I need to mix things up a bit,” or “because I can’t stop thinking about how bad the All-In podcast is,” or “because I have two hours right now before a doctor’s appointment and Sam is at a conference so when I get back she will be busy so can’t edit.” I wanted to write my take about the All-In podcast because it got me really riled up, but it came when it did because an investigation I’m working on needs a bit more time, and we’re shorthanded this week, with some folks traveling, myself dealing with a bunch of life logistics, reporting for longer term things, a doctor’s appointment that runs longer than expected, whatever. I know 99% of you know this and are here with us but basically: If you’re waiting in line for more of the original reason you subscribed to us, PLEASE STAY IN LINE. I promise we have not drastically changed our editorial remit, our perspectives, or what we care about because we haven’t done an article about surveillance in a week. We are possibly just working on the next big thing in that space, are trying to follow the news or current events to some degree, or, like, one of our moms is visiting us so we had to skip a specific story.

We obviously can’t and don’t explain that on every article we do as it is not interesting to the vast majority of people and all of our articles need to stand on their own. But yeah, we do a mix of stuff for all sorts of reasons both philosophical and highly practical and logistical.
